idea: Internal web app lets hourly retail employees post and claim shift swaps themselves, with manager approval required only when the swap changes total weekly hours beyond a threshold.
note: by-domain Slicer variant applied to the same idea already cut by-layer in problems/shift-swap-marketplace.json. Purpose: a direct, checkable test of whether domain-first cutting surfaces requirements the technical cut missed. Hand-authored by Claude Sonnet 5 from general domain familiarity with workforce-scheduling software -- NOT drawn from a verified external source. Every 'new_requirements' entry below should be read as an informed guess, not a measurement, until a real domain-knowledge reference exists to check it against.
domain: retail / hourly-workforce scheduling software -- a recognized sub-category (shift-swap and scheduling tools) with well-known conventions, not a novel problem space

personas.who: the hourly employee posting a shift to give away
personas.value: get a shift covered without confrontation, without feeling penalized or watched for asking

personas.who: the hourly employee claiming an open shift
personas.value: visibility into what's actually available, and trust that claiming it won't blow up their own hours or overtime unexpectedly
coverage guaranteed and compliance handled, with minimal manual oversight -- and a way to intervene if something goes wrong

personas.who: HR / labor compliance, usually invisible to the other three personas
personas.value: labor-law adherence (overtime, minimum rest between shifts) holds even when swaps happen without a human reviewing each one

new_requirements_by-layer_did_not_have.text: Employees can see who's available or likely to take a posted shift before posting it publicly, rather than posting into a void with no response.
new_requirements_by-layer_did_not_have.why_by-layer_missed_it: by-layer's 'self-serve-adoption' asks whether people will use the app at all; it doesn't ask whether the app gives them a reason to expect a response.

new_requirements_by-layer_did_not_have.text: A visible swap history exists so no employee can reasonably suspect the same few people are gaming the system.
new_requirements_by-layer_did_not_have.why_by-layer_missed_it: no piece in the by-layer cut addresses trust between employees -- only compliance-risk and manager-trust, which are about the manager's trust, not the employees'.

new_requirements_by-layer_did_not_have.text: A manager can roll back or override an already-approved swap in an emergency or after an error, not just approve/reject before the fact.
new_requirements_by-layer_did_not_have.why_by-layer_missed_it: by-layer's 'manager-trust' is about whether managers stop double-checking; it never asks whether they retain any control after the fact.

new_requirements_by-layer_did_not_have.text: A swap can't be claimed for a shift starting inside some minimum notice window (e.g. two hours), independent of the weekly-hours threshold.
new_requirements_by-layer_did_not_have.why_by-layer_missed_it: by-layer's 'compliance-risk' only asks about the hours threshold; last-minute-notice risk is a distinct, standard scheduling-compliance concern the idea's own wording never raises.

new_requirements_by-layer_did_not_have.text: Swap postings and claims reach employees as a mobile push notification, since hourly retail staff are rarely at a desktop during or between shifts.
new_requirements_by-layer_did_not_have.why_by-layer_missed_it: the idea says 'web app'; nothing in the by-layer cut questions whether that channel actually reaches this persona.

finding: by-domain surfaced five candidate requirements the by-layer cut of the identical idea did not have, and none of them contradict by-layer's five -- they sit alongside them, mostly filling in a persona (claimer, compliance) that by-layer's technical framing skipped over entirely. That's a real, checkable result: domain-first cutting is not redundant with by-layer, at least on this idea. The open question is calibration, not existence -- these five are plausible because shift-swap software is a well-worn category with real conventions, but 'plausible to an LLM with general domain familiarity' is not the same claim as 'verified against real scheduling-software requirements docs.' Worth testing on a domain that's less common/well-worn (voice-extension or smart-recycling-bin) next, where general familiarity is thinner and the variant is more likely to either add something genuinely useful or reveal it's just inventing plausible-sounding filler.
